title: What you'd want for yourself
hookLine: none of you truly believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself (Bukhari; Nawawi 13)

cards: Two slices of cake are left, and one is plainly bigger. Somebody has to cut, and somebody has to choose. Families have a trick for this: whoever cuts picks last.
Suddenly the knife gets very careful. Nobody gave a speech about fairness. The cutter simply has to treat the other slice as if it might be theirs.
A short saying in the Islamic tradition asks for something like that, only it reaches past cake, all the way into faith itself.

teach.b: The saying comes from the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, in the hadith collection of al-Bukhari, and the scholar al-Nawawi later placed it thirteenth in his little book of forty hadith.
In plain words: none of you truly believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself. It's short enough to fit on a sticky note.
Notice where it puts the test. Not none of you is polite, or generous: none of you truly believes. In this hadith, faith isn't finished in private.
It shows up in what you wish for the person beside you.
And notice the measuring stick. It isn't some ideal you have to look up. It's you.

You already know what you'd want: to be forgiven quickly, given the benefit of the doubt, to have your name said kindly when you're not in the room. The saying takes that private wish list and turns it outward.
Then the word brother. Some readers hear a fellow Muslim; others hear any fellow human being. This lesson won't settle it.
Either way, the circle of what you want for yourself gets bigger by one. The Hebrew Bible has a neighbor in it too. Leviticus says, "thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself."
Two scriptures, each saying it in its own words.

how: Muslims learn this hadith early, often from al-Nawawi's collection of forty hadith, and it is commonly memorized and quoted as a summary of how faith should show in the way a person treats others.

o: the hadith collection that holds this saying
the scholar who ranked forty hadith in order
a Quran chapter about loving your neighbor

games.q: who said what about the person beside you — tap the pairs.
p: placed it thirteenth in his forty

s: the hadith says none of you is generous until...
it says none of you truly believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself.
the measure in the saying is your own wish for yourself
you already know what you'd want; the saying turns it outward.
every reader takes brother to mean only a fellow Muslim
some readers hear a fellow Muslim, others hear any fellow human being.

games.q: two slices of cake, one bigger. you're cutting, and you pick last. what does the cutter do?
o: cut quickly and hope for the best.
cut carefully, as if the other slice might be theirs.
games.why: when the cutter picks last, they treat the other slice as their own. the hadith asks for that, only about everything.

practice: Bring to mind one good thing you want for yourself right now: rest, maybe, or a hard conversation going well, or being understood.

Then picture one person close by, at home, at work or down the street, and see that same good thing arriving for them, no smaller slice. If you pray, you can hold that person in your own tradition's words.

wordCard.voice: Al-Bukhari. The hadith collection holding the Prophet's saying that none of you truly believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: (that) he loves, the verb the hadith uses twice: for his brother, and for himself.

carryVoice: Your line: what I'd want. The measuring stick was you all along. That's plenty for today.

sources.q: thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself
